title: Price, physical availability, and economic activity
description: Three synchronized panels place supply and inventory proxies beside oil-price and delivered-energy-cost momentum, then beside real activity and demand.
plainLanguageSummary: Use the three panels to inspect episodes where physical tightness, delivered energy costs, and economic activity move in different directions. A falling benchmark price is not, by itself, evidence that energy has become easy to afford.
howToRead: The lines are standardized within their fixed reference period so their timing can be compared without putting unrelated units on one axis. Read the panels together and inspect the exact observations in the table.

calculation.formula: Each panel uses fixed-reference z = (observation - reference-period mean) / reference-period standard deviation; inventory tightness = -CI_zscore.
calculation.explanation: The panels retain synchronized dates while keeping physical, price, and activity units separate. Falling benchmark prices can reflect demand destruction rather than abundant or affordable energy.
calculation.example: A value at date t uses only observations dated t or earlier unless the chart explicitly labels a visual shift.

patternsToWatch: Price declines coinciding with weakening production, spending, or employment
Delivered energy inflation remaining elevated after benchmark oil momentum fades
Inventory tightness and refinery utilization diverging from domestic production growth
limitations: These are U.S. indicators and do not measure global physical availability or every delivered fuel cost.
Supply shocks, policy, exchange rates, credit conditions, and common recession drivers can move several panels together.
The synchronized view is descriptive; it does not establish the affordability feedback loop as a causal model.
sourceNotes: EIA Monthly Energy Review and WPULEUS3
